common_name: Emerald Heights Distylium (Upright Evergreen Screening Shrub for Shade)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; its upright, columnar growth habit makes it a shade-tolerant substitute for narrow evergreen screens where boxwood or holly would struggle in wet or shaded ground.

directions: Emerald Heights is an upright, narrow-growing distylium selection bred for tight hedges and screens, holding a columnar shape without the wide spread of older, mounding distylium cultivars. Its small, glossy, dark evergreen leaves stay clean through heat, humidity, and periodic wet soil, and inconspicuous reddish flowers appear in late winter without seed litter or maintenance concerns. As a hybrid derived from wetland-tolerant Asian Distylium species, it tolerates both boggy, poorly drained soil and average garden conditions, and shrugs off the deer browsing that plagues many broadleaf evergreens. Plant in partial shade to full sun and give it minimal pruning beyond an annual shaping, since its naturally tidy form needs little correction.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; unlike Skimmia japonica, Reeves Skimmia carries perfect flowers on every plant, so a single specimen sets its own dull-red berries without a separate pollinator.

directions: Reeves Skimmia is a low, mounding evergreen shrub for deep shade, valued for glossy dark leaves, fragrant creamy-white spring flower clusters, and dull-red berries that persist through winter — all on a single, self-pollinating plant, unlike the dioecious Skimmia japonica, which needs separate male and female plants to fruit. It performs best in the dappled or full shade of a woodland garden, where sun and heat would scorch its foliage, and prefers consistently moist, acidic, well-drained soil rich in organic matter. Its compact, slow-growing habit suits foundation plantings on the shaded side of a house, mass plantings under trees, or mixed borders alongside hostas, ferns, and hellebores. It needs only minimal pruning to remove any damaged wood, and is rarely bothered by pests once established in the shaded, humus-rich site it prefers.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Sonic Bloom Pearl Weigela (Reblooming Pale Pink-Blush Weigela)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; deadhead the heavy spring flush lightly to help trigger the later summer and fall rebloom cycles typical of the Sonic Bloom series.

directions: Sonic Bloom Pearl carries the softest coloring in the Sonic Bloom weigela series, opening pale blush-pink and fading toward creamy white as each flower ages, giving a gentler, two-tone look on the shrub compared to its more saturated Sonic Bloom Pink and Sonic Bloom Red siblings. Like the rest of the series it reblooms on new growth through summer and into fall rather than flowering only in a single spring flush, keeping hummingbirds visiting for months longer than older weigela cultivars. Give it full sun for the best rebloom and well-drained soil, and limit pruning to light shaping right after the initial spring flush so the wood that carries later flushes is not removed. It otherwise tolerates heat, humidity, and average garden soil with little maintenance.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: October Magic Bride Camellia (White Formal Double Reblooming Sasanqua)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; its compact, upright habit fits a foundation bed or large container better than older, sprawling sasanqua types.

directions: October Magic Bride is a Southern Living Plant Collection sasanqua bred for fully formal double, pure white blooms with a soft pink blush at the petal base, opening over an extended fall-into-winter window on a dense, compact frame. Its clean, glossy evergreen foliage and heavy bud set make it a strong choice for a shaded foundation planting or as a specimen near an entry where its cool-season flowers stand out against darker evergreen backdrops. As with all camellias, give it consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil and a protective mulch layer over its shallow roots, and prune only lightly right after flowering so next season's flower buds are not removed.

common_name: October Magic Pink Perplexion Camellia (Ruffled Bicolor Pink Sasanqua)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.5-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun.

directions: October Magic Pink Perplexion is a Southern Living Plant Collection sasanqua named for its ruffled, semi-double to double blooms that mix two shades of pink on the same flower, giving a variegated, almost painterly look unusual among camellias. It flowers heavily through fall and into winter on a dense, upright plant with glossy dark evergreen leaves that provide year-round structure to a partly shaded bed. Give it consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil, a protective mulch layer over its shallow root system, and only light pruning right after bloom, since flower buds for the following season form on the current year's growth. Its cool-season color makes it a strong companion to hellebores and other winter-interest shade perennials.
